q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkane shown?
h: Find every seven-carbon chain. When two chains tie in length, pick the one carrying more substituents; then number for the lowest locant set and list prefixes alphabetically.
w: Two different seven-carbon chains exist: one runs through the ethyl branch, the other through the isopropyl end. When chains tie in length, the parent is the one with more substituents. Running through the isopropyl end gives three substituents (methyl, ethyl, methyl), while running through the ethyl gives only two. Numbering from the isopropyl end gives locants {2,3,5}, lower than {3,5,6} from the other end. Prefixes are listed alphabetically, with di/tri ignored, so ethyl comes before methyl: 3-ethyl-2,5-dimethylheptane.
x: The locants are right, but prefixes must be listed alphabetically (ethyl before methyl). The multiplier “di” does not count when alphabetizing.
This numbers from the wrong end. {3,5,6} loses to {2,3,5} at the first point of difference.
This heptane chain runs through the ethyl group and carries only two substituents. Among equally long chains, the one with more substituents is the parent.

q: A student names a compound “2-ethylpentane.” What is the correct IUPAC name for the structure the student had in mind?
h: Draw the structure the student described, then look for a longer continuous chain.
w: Draw it: a pentane chain with CH2CH3 on C2. Following the ethyl branch gives a six-carbon chain, so the parent is hexane, not pentane. The one-carbon branch (the old C1 of pentane) then sits on C3 of the hexane chain when numbered from the nearer end: 3-methylhexane. An ethyl group on C2 always signals a missed longer chain.
x: An ethyl group on C2 extends the chain by two carbons, so pentane is not the longest chain and the name is wrong.
This numbers the hexane from the far end. The methyl must get the lowest locant, 3.
3-Ethylpentane is a different isomer of C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>: its ethyl is on the central carbon, so no longer chain exists. The student's ethyl is on C2, which creates a six-carbon chain.

q: Which name describes the compound shown, including its relative configuration?
h: Decide whether the two groups point to the same face of the ring (both wedged or both dashed). With a tie in locants, the group cited first alphabetically gets C1.
w: The two ring bonds to the substituents use the same wedge/dash sense, so both groups are on the same face: cis. The ring locants are {1,3} either way, so the tie is broken alphabetically: ethyl is cited first and gets C1. The name is cis-1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane.
x: Both substituents are drawn on the same face of the ring, which is cis. Trans would need one wedge and one dash.
Prefixes are cited in alphabetical order, so ethyl comes before methyl in the name.
When the locant set ties ({1,3} both ways), the alphabetically first prefix (ethyl) gets the lower number, C1.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the alkene shown?
h: Two five-carbon chains contain the C=C. Choose the one with more substituents, then rank the groups on each alkene carbon by CIP rules.
w: Both five-carbon chains contain the double bond (one runs into the ethyl group, one into the isopropyl group). The tie is broken by the number of substituents: the chain through the isopropyl carbon carries an ethyl and a methyl (two) versus one isopropyl group for the other chain. Number from the end nearer the C=C: pent-2-ene with 3-ethyl and 4-methyl. For E/Z: on C2, CH3 > H; on C3, CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) > CH2CH3 (C,H,H). The CH3 on C2 and the isopropyl carbon are on the same side, so the alkene is (Z)-3-ethyl-4-methylpent-2-ene.
x: The higher-priority groups (CH<sub>3</sub> on C2 and the isopropyl carbon on C3) are on the same side of the double bond, which is Z.
This chain is as long but carries only one substituent. With equal chains, the parent is the one with more substituents.
The double bond must get the lowest locant, so numbering starts at the CH<sub>3</sub>CH= end (pent-2-ene, not pent-3-ene).

q: How many degrees of unsaturation (rings + π bonds) does a compound with formula C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>10</sub>ClNO<sub>2</sub> have?
h: Treat a halogen like H, ignore O, and let each N add one to the H count allowed.
w: DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 = (18 + 2 + 1 − 10 − 1)/2 = 10/2 = 5. Oxygen does not change the count. 4-Chlorophenylalanine (a benzene ring, 4, plus a C=O, 1) is one compound with this formula.
x: This comes from subtracting the nitrogen instead of adding it. Each N raises the number of H atoms a saturated molecule can hold by one.
This treats Cl as if it did not count. A halogen takes the place of an H, so it is subtracted like H.
This counts oxygen as if it lowered the H count. Divalent O does not change the DBE.

q: Capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot, is shown. Which functional group is not present in capsaicin?
h: Look at what is attached to each oxygen and to the carbonyl carbon.
w: Go group by group. The C=O carbon is bonded to N, so that unit is an amide (a secondary amide, N–H). The OH sits directly on the benzene ring, which makes it a phenol. The OCH3 on the ring is an aryl methyl ether. There is also a trans C=C. No carbonyl carbon is bonded to an O–C, so there is no ester.
x: The C(=O)–NH unit is an amide; capsaicin has one.
The OH bonded directly to the aromatic ring is a phenol; capsaicin has one.
The CH<sub>3</sub>O– group on the ring is an ether (an aryl methyl ether); capsaicin has one.

q: Cocaine is shown. Which choice correctly lists its functional groups (ignore the benzene ring)?
c: two esters and a tertiary amine
two esters and a secondary amine
an ester, a ketone, and a tertiary amine
an ester, an ether, and a tertiary amide
h: For each C=O, ask what the carbonyl carbon is bonded to. For the nitrogen, count its carbon neighbors and check whether any is a C=O.
w: Both carbonyl carbons are bonded to an O–C: one is a methyl ester (CO2CH3) and one is a benzoate ester. The nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and a CH3) and none is a carbonyl carbon, so it is a tertiary amine. Answer: two esters and a tertiary amine.
x: The N carries a CH<sub>3</sub> and two ring carbons, three carbon groups in all, which makes it tertiary.
Neither carbonyl carbon is flanked by two carbons; each is bonded to an oxygen that carries a carbon, so both are esters.
The nitrogen is not bonded to a carbonyl carbon, so it is an amine, not an amide; and the O–C single bonds belong to esters, not a simple ether.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the bicyclic compound shown?
h: Count the carbons in each bridge between the two bridgeheads. Number from a bridgehead around the longest bridge, then the next longest, and the shortest bridge last.
w: The bridgeheads are joined by bridges of 3, 2 and 1 carbons (8 carbons total), so the ring system is bicyclo[3.2.1]octane, with the numbers in decreasing order. Numbering starts at a bridgehead (C1), runs around the 3-carbon bridge (C2–C4) to the other bridgehead (C5), continues through the 2-carbon bridge (C6, C7) and ends on the 1-carbon bridge (C8). The methyl is on the 2-carbon bridge next to a bridgehead. Choosing C1 so that this carbon is reached first in the 2-carbon bridge gives it locant 6 (the other choice gives 7): 6-methylbicyclo[3.2.1]octane.
x: This starts at the wrong bridgehead. Both numberings are allowed by the bridge order, so pick the one giving the methyl the lower locant, 6.
C2–C4 belong to the longest (3-carbon) bridge. The methyl is on the 2-carbon bridge, which is numbered after the 3-carbon bridge.
Bridge sizes are cited in decreasing order: [3.2.1], not [2.3.1].

q: Which structure is (R)-4-chloropent-1-ene?
h: First find structures with the right chain and Cl position (C=C at C1, Cl at C4). Then assign R/S at C4: Cl > CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> > CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: Only two choices have five chain carbons with C=C at C1–C2 and Cl at C4. At C4 the priorities are Cl > CH2CH=CH2 > CH3 > H. Viewed with H pointing away, Cl → CH2CH=CH2 → CH3 must run clockwise for R; only one of those two structures does. Its mirror image is the S enantiomer.
x: This is the enantiomer, (S)-4-chloropent-1-ene: the Cl is on the opposite wedge/dash.
The Cl here is on C3, next to the double bond: this is (R)-3-chloropent-1-ene.
This chain has six carbons: (R)-4-chlorohex-1-ene, not a pentene.

q: What is the IUPAC (substitutive) name of the ether shown?
h: Name the larger alkyl group as the parent alkane and the smaller one as an alkoxy prefix.
w: The oxygen joins an ethyl group and an isopropyl group. The larger group (three carbons) is the parent, propane; the smaller becomes the ethoxy prefix. The O is on the middle carbon of propane: 2-ethoxypropane (common name ethyl isopropyl ether).
x: 1-Ethoxypropane has the O on the end carbon of a straight propyl group; here the O is on the central CH carbon.
That compound has a methyl on oxygen and a four-carbon chain; the drawing has an O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group and a three-carbon branch.
The parent here has only three carbons. A butane parent would need four carbons on one side of the oxygen.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the amine shown?
h: The parent is the longest carbon chain attached to N. The other groups on N are named with the prefix N-.
w: The nitrogen carries two CH3 groups and a four-carbon sec-butyl group. The longest carbon chain bonded to N is butane, with N on C2 when numbered from the nearer end. The two methyls on nitrogen are cited as N,N-dimethyl: N,N-dimethylbutan-2-amine.
x: The amine suffix must get the lowest possible locant: 2, not 3.
This is an isomer: it has an ethyl and a methyl on N and an isopropyl group. The drawn compound has two N-methyls and a four-carbon chain.
This uses a three-carbon parent and treats a chain carbon as a methyl branch. The parent must be the longest chain, butane.

q: How many degrees of unsaturation does the compound shown have?
h: Each ring counts 1, each double bond 1 and each triple bond 2. Check your count with the formula.
w: Count: one ring (1) + one C=C (1) + the C≡C (2) + the C≡N (2) = 6. Check with the formula C9H9N: (18 + 2 + 1 − 9)/2 = 6.
x: This misses one unit, usually by counting the ring C=C but forgetting the ring itself, or by counting a triple bond as one.
This counts each triple bond as only one degree. A triple bond has two π bonds and counts 2.
This double-counts something. One ring + one C=C + two triple bonds (2 each) gives 6.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Pick the longest chain containing the C=C; Cl is only a prefix. For E/Z, compare the two groups on each alkene carbon by first atoms, then the atoms attached.
w: The longest chain containing the double bond runs CH3–CH=C–CH2CH2CH3 (six carbons), numbered so the C=C gets locant 2. The CH2Cl on C3 is a chloromethyl prefix. On C2, CH3 > H. On C3, CH2Cl outranks the propyl group because its first atom bears (Cl,H,H) versus (C,H,H). The CH3 on C2 and the CH2Cl are on opposite sides, so the alkene is E, even though the main chain itself is drawn cis: (E)-3-(chloromethyl)hex-2-ene.
x: Z would require the two top-priority groups on the same side. Here the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl, not the propyl chain, is the higher-priority group on C3, and it is opposite the CH<sub>3</sub>.
The double bond must get the lowest locant, so number from the CH<sub>3</sub>CH= end (hex-2-ene).
This parent has only five carbons. Halogens are prefixes and do not have to be in the parent chain, so the six-carbon chain wins.

q: The enyne shown gives its multiple bonds the same locants from either end of the chain. What is its correct IUPAC name?
h: Give the multiple bonds, taken together, the lowest locants. If both directions tie, the double bond gets the lower number.
w: Numbering from the alkene end puts the multiple bonds at {1,5}; numbering from the alkyne end also gives {1,5}. When the ene/yne set ties, the rule gives the double bond the lower locant, so C1 is the CH2= carbon. The methyl is then on C4: 4-methylhex-1-en-5-yne. This rule outranks the substituent locant, so the methyl does not get 3.
x: This gives the alkyne locant 1. With a tie in the multiple-bond set, the double bond gets the lower number.
With the C=C at C1, the methyl lands on C4, not C3. Count again from the CH<sub>2</sub>= end.
With the C≡C at C1, the methyl would be on C3. In any case the alkyne end should not be C1 here.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number so the double bond gets the lowest locant, list halogens alphabetically, then rank each alkene carbon's two groups by atomic number.
w: The double bond must be at C1, so C1 is the CHCl carbon and C2 bears Br and the ethyl group. Prefixes are listed alphabetically: bromo before chloro. On C1, Cl > H; on C2, Br > CH2CH3. Cl and Br are on the same side, so the alkene is Z: (Z)-2-bromo-1-chlorobut-1-ene.
x: Cl and Br, the higher-priority atoms on each alkene carbon, are on the same side. That is Z.
The prefixes must be in alphabetical order: bromo before chloro.
This numbers from the wrong end. The double bond must get the lowest locant, 1.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: OH is the principal group, so it is the suffix and its carbon must be in the parent chain, lowest locant. For E/Z, compare CH<sub>2</sub>OH and isopropyl atom by atom.
w: The OH is the principal characteristic group, so the parent must contain the CH2OH carbon and the name ends in -ol. From that carbon, two four-carbon chains are possible; the one containing the C=C is preferred (more multiple bonds). Number from the OH carbon: but-2-en-1-ol with an isopropyl group on C2. For E/Z, on C2: CH2OH (O,H,H) beats CH(CH3)2 (C,C,H) at the first point of difference, because O > C. On C3: CH3 > H. CH2OH and CH3 are on the same side: (Z)-2-isopropylbut-2-en-1-ol.
x: The isopropyl group has more carbons, but CIP compares atoms one at a time: CH<sub>2</sub>OH carries an O, which beats the C,C,H set of isopropyl. The top groups are on the same side, so Z.
An alcohol is named with the -ol suffix, not as a hydroxy- prefix, and its carbon must be in the parent chain.
The OH carbon must get the lowest locant (C1), not C4.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: The OH carbon is C1. Go around the ring in the direction that gives the double bond the lower locant.
w: The alcohol is the principal group, so the OH carbon is C1. Going toward the C=C gives the double bond locants 2,3 (cyclohex-2-ene); the other direction gives 5,6. The methyl then sits on C3: 3-methylcyclohex-2-en-1-ol.
x: The OH carbon must be C1 because the alcohol is the suffix. Here the alkene was numbered first.
This numbers around the ring the long way. The double bond should get the lower locants, 2 and 3.
Here the methyl would be on the C=C carbon next to C1. In the drawing it is on the far alkene carbon, C3.

q: What is the complete IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Assign each center separately. At C2: Cl > C3 (bears Br) > CH<sub>3</sub> > H. At C3: Br > C2 (bears Cl) > CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: Numbering from the left gives locants {2,3}; from the right {3,4}, so the Cl carbon is C2 and the Br carbon is C3 (bromo is cited first alphabetically). At C2: Cl > C3 (Br,C,H) > CH3 > H; as drawn this center is R. At C3: Br > C2 (Cl,C,H) > CH2CH3 > H; also R. Name: (2R,3R)-3-bromo-2-chloropentane.
x: Both descriptors are reversed. This is the enantiomer; recheck which way the H points before reading the direction.
C2 is right but C3 is not. At C3 the C2 branch (Cl,C,H) outranks the ethyl group (C,H,H).
C3 is right but C2 is not. At C2 the C3 branch, which carries Br, outranks CH<sub>3</sub>, and the result is R.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: Number the bicyclic system first (C1 bridgehead, then the longer bridges, the one-carbon bridge last). Among the allowed numberings, the double bond gets the lowest locants before the substituent.
w: The ring system is bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (bridges of 2, 2 and 1 carbon). The double bond comes before the substituent in numbering, so the C=C is placed at C2–C3. That leaves two choices of starting bridgehead. Starting at the bridgehead not next to the methyl carbon, the numbering runs C2=C3, C4 (bridgehead), C5 (methyl carbon), C6, and C7 (one-carbon bridge). The other start puts the methyl on C6. Lowest locant: 5-methylbicyclo[2.2.1]hept-2-ene.
x: This starts at the other bridgehead. Both numberings put the C=C at C2, so choose the one giving the methyl the lower locant, 5.
The double bond takes precedence over the substituent for low locants, so it must be at C2, not C5.
C7 is the one-carbon bridge. The methyl in the drawing is on a two-carbon bridge.

q: Which structure is cis-1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane?
h: First check the positions (1,3 means one carbon between them). Then check that both groups are on the same face (both wedged or both dashed).
w: Two choices are 1,3-disubstituted and two are 1,2. Of the 1,3 pair, the correct one has Br and CH3 on the same face of the ring (both wedges or both dashes), which is cis.
x: This is the 1,3 compound with Br and CH3 on opposite faces: trans-1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane.
The groups are on adjacent carbons: this is cis-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
The groups are on adjacent carbons and on opposite faces: trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane.
